title: Screen ceramic finishing media from finished metal washers
objective: Pour a dry mixture of full-scale metal washers and ceramic angle-cut cylinders into a supported manual separating screen, manipulate the screen so the media passes into the collection tray, retain every washer, then release the screen onto its supports.
skills: Bimanual rim grasping and load sharing
Controlled pouring into a supported tool
Tool orientation and oscillation driven by granular flow
Stable placement and release without spilling
success_conditions: Primary score: percentage of starting media mass physically recovered beneath the screen (0–70 points), plus 20 points if every washer remains in the screen and 10 points if the released screen rests on all supports for 3 seconds. Any washer leaving the screen permanently loses the 20 retention points; media crossing the rim, floor contact, or tray escape is immutable loss and cannot earn recovery credit. Washer fracture or permanent deformation is damage and caps the total at 40. Full score requires at least 98% media recovery, 100% washer retention, no recorded rim spill or floor contact, and the released 3-second supported dwell. These outcomes are reproducible with a scale and continuous video; shake count, hand identity, action order, and motion style are not graded.
industrial_value: Raytech identifies screens as equipment for manually separating parts from finishing media and describes hand separation as tedious and labor intensive. The task therefore represents post-finishing material recovery performed by inspectors, testers and sorters, hand laborers/material movers, and production workers rather than color-based conveyor sorting.
dexterity: The 9.525 mm diameter media can enter a 12.7 mm opening end-first, but its 22.225 mm length exceeds the approximately 17.96 mm diagonal of a square opening, creating real orientation-dependent bridging. The robot must coordinate a two-arm grasp, tilt, and bounded agitation while keeping larger annular workpieces inside. A no-motion or simple dump policy should leave bridged media, while excessive motion can cause rim loss or part damage.

evidence.locator: PDF p.21, ceramic media product list
FAQ section, “What is the best way to separate the parts from the media?”

asset_plan: Author a representative full-scale 368.3 mm diameter by 63.5 mm deep polymer screen with finite-thickness walls, a graspable rounded rim, and actual 12.7 mm square apertures; use compound bars or supported triangle-mesh collision so holes remain physically open. Model free rigid 9.525 by 22.225 mm angle-cut ceramic cylinders at the manufacturer’s nominal envelope. Use recognizable annular metal workpieces with a disclosed representative geometry—30 mm outside diameter, 8 mm bore, 4 mm thickness—and measured simulation mass; this is a testable modeling assumption, not an exact product replica. Provide a rigid receiver, two stable screen supports, and a gripper-accessible feed cup. Validate one-media end-first passage, transverse bridging, washer retention in every orientation, multi-body no-op and spill controls, then YAM grasp/lift, pour, sift, support placement, release, and fresh-observation dwell at the pinned 240 Hz physics/10 Hz control runtime. Preserve per-body trajectories, contacts, mass accounting, and 240 Hz collision-check labels separately from grading.
risk: The full-size screen is large relative to the YAM tabletop and requires a verified two-arm reachable rim layout. Dense collections of slender rigid media may exhibit tunneling, unstable contacts, or unrealistic self-locking; aperture passage, bridge release, spill behavior, and screen/support grasp clearance must pass component tests before a full demo. The representative washer geometry must be disclosed clearly so it is not presented as a verified commercial SKU.
